disclaimer: Reminder reference only — NOT legal authority. Season dates, zones, quotas and limits are set annually and can change. Always verify current regulations with Alberta Forestry and Parks (Fish and Wildlife) before trapping. Trapping in Alberta is governed by the Wildlife Act and the Wildlife Regulation (Alberta Regulation 143/1997); the Alberta Guide to Trapping Regulations is a plain-language summary of the Regulation, not the law itself. Report violations to Report A Poacher at 1-800-642-3800.

license_summary.certified_traps: Alberta has adopted the AIHTS certified-trap list in law: Wildlife Regulation s. 107.1 incorporates Phase 1 of the Fur Institute of Canada's 'Certified Traps – AIHTS Implementation' list by reference, and a person shall not use any trap for a certified species unless it is currently listed by name and certified for that species. The list is published annually in the Guide to Trapping Regulations. New for 2026/27: certified cage and box traps are mandatory for raccoon; certified foothold restraining traps for coyote become mandatory in 2028/29.
license_summary.course: First-time trappers — anyone who has never held a trapping licence in Alberta or elsewhere, or who has not completed a fur management course — must successfully complete the Alberta Trapper Education Course and pass a test on humane trapping and fur management before being licensed. Course information: Alberta Trappers' Association, Box 6020, Westlock, AB T7P 2P7, phone 780-349-6626, albertatrappers.com/trapper-courses.html.
license_summary.fees: Resident Fur Management Licence $20; Registered Fur Management Licence, senior holder, $40 plus an area fee of $10 for each 36 sq mi of RFMA area in excess of 72 sq mi, plus $10 for any remaining area, to a maximum area fee of $40 (the Guide presents the same fee as $10/$20/$30/$40 for RFMAs of 3/4/5/6 townships; the maximum combined licence and area fee is $80); Registered FML partner $20; Indian Fur Management Licence free; Métis Fur Management Licence — no fee stated in the Guide; Damage Control Licence — no fee stated. Fur dealer permits: Class 1 $100, Class 2 $500. Listed fees do not include GST. $5 from each Registered FML funds the Alberta Trappers' Compensation Program. (Guide, Licence Fees; cross-checked against Wildlife Regulation, Schedule 8, Part 3 — the two agree exactly.)
license_summary.harvest_report: Registered FML holders must submit the Registered Fur Harvest Report (Form WA12) with the annual licence renewal by September 30, covering the species and number of all furbearers harvested on their RFMA(s), including harvest by their spouse and resident children under 18. Resident FML holders are asked to complete the Resident Fur Harvest Report (Form WA12A), by WMU, on or before September 30. New for 2026-27: senior RFML holders are requested to submit completed trapping activity reports (logbooks) to the Alberta Furbearer Harvest and Trapping Effort Program (online at atalogbook.ab-conservation.com; a pull-out logbook is included in the centre of the printed Guide). Fur Harvest Reports remain required for annual renewal.
license_summary.licence_types: Registered Fur Management Licence (senior holder or partner) — for a Registered Fur Management Area; Resident Fur Management Licence — private lands the holder owns, leases or occupies, or other private land with Form WA 19A permission; Indian Fur Management Licence — First Nation individuals within their First Nation boundaries, issued by Band Administration Offices; Métis Fur Management Licence — Métis Settlement members within their settlement, issued by Métis Settlement Supervisors; Damage Control Licence — for problem wildlife not covered by the no-licence authorities.
license_summary.licensing_transition: Since July 2021, all fur management licences are issued through AlbertaRELM and require a WiN (Wildlife Identification Number) activation ($8 + GST). Vacant RFMAs are listed at, and applied for through, Fish and Wildlife District Offices.
license_summary.non_licence_animals: Raccoon and skunk are classed as non-licence animals: they may be hunted or trapped during all seasons by the owner or occupant of land, a person authorized by the owner or occupant, or the holder of a licence authorizing the trapping of furbearers (Wildlife Regulation, Schedule 1, s. 7(12)). The open season for hunting non-licence animals is January 1 to December 31, except in Big Game Zone 17, where there is no open season (Schedule 15, s. 12).
license_summary.permission: A Resident Fur Management Licence holder trapping on private land they do not own, lease or occupy must carry the licence together with Form WA 19A, the landowner's signed written authorization to hunt fur-bearing animals, and produce both on the request of a Fish and Wildlife Officer. Use of neck snares for wolf, coyote, fox and bobcat on another person's land requires the landowner's additional written authorization (Form WA 19A provides for it).
license_summary.problem_wildlife: Without a licence (Wildlife Regulation, Schedule 1, s. 7; Guide, Control of Problem Wildlife): beaver may be hunted and trapped year-round on private land by the owner or occupant or a resident with written permission; badger and red squirrel may be hunted or trapped year-round by a resident on private land with a right of access; muskrat may be hunted year-round on private land (owner/occupant, or resident with written authorization); red fox may be hunted (not trapped) year-round by a resident on private land with a right of access; coyote may be hunted (not trapped) year-round province-wide by residents with a right of access, landowners/occupants and livestock keepers (pelts must be salvaged when hunting under a livestock keeper's written authorization on Green Area lands); wolf may be hunted (not trapped) year-round on private land, and by livestock keepers on public land, extending to land within 8 km (5 mi) of that land; raccoon and skunk may be hunted or trapped year-round by landowners/occupants, their authorized persons, or licensed trappers; bobcat may be hunted (not trapped) by residents from November 1 to the last day of February in WMUs 102, 104, 106, 108, 112, 116, 118, 119 and part of WMU 110; rabbit and hare may be hunted year-round without a licence on land with a right of access, and snared by residents with single-strand wire snares. A Damage Control Licence may be necessary for other species destroying property.
license_summary.quotas: The Alberta season table (Guide p. 15; Wildlife Regulation, Schedule 15, Table 5) sets NO daily, possession or season bag limits for any furbearer. Instead, the Minister may set an open season quota — the maximum number of otter, wolverine, lynx and fisher that may be killed in a Registered Fur Management Area during the open season (Schedule 15, s. 8.7). A quota that is set must immediately be made publicly available on a department website, and when the quota is reached in an RFMA the open season no longer applies there (Schedule 15, s. 9(1)(b)). The 2026-27 Guide does not print quota numbers — guides up to at least 2018-19 printed an RFMA limits table (a basic limit per RFMA plus per-township increments for fisher, lynx, otter and wolverine), which is absent from the 2025-26 and 2026-27 Guides — and current quota values were not located in this pass; they are recorded as a known gap.
license_summary.registration_tagging: Mandatory registration: fisher, lynx, otter and wolverine killed in an open season must be registered within 30 days of the close of that season (killed outside an open season, within 30 days of the kill), and in all cases before sale, processing or export, by presenting the pelt at a Fish and Wildlife District Office or approved location. All bobcat taken under any authority must be registered before the skin is sold, processed or exported from Alberta, or within 30 days after harvest. Wolverine registration requires the skull with the pelt (tooth and DNA sample). Any cougar harvest, including an accidental capture, must be registered at a district office immediately. A provincial export permit is required to export any furbearer skin or pelt from Alberta (exceptions include beaver castor and oil glands, claws, skulls and teeth of furbearers, processed skins, and lawfully possessed coyote skins), and a CITES permit is required to export wolf, lynx, bobcat, otter or black bear across an international boundary. Raw skins may be sold only to a licensed fur dealer; dealers verify a partner's licence and WA188 card, record lynx, fisher, wolverine and otter on a Furbearers Registration Certificate (Form WA324), report monthly, and retain records for two years. Exception: non-residents within 30 miles of Fort Smith, NWT, trapping on an RFMA wholly north of the north boundary of Township 118 and east of Wood Buffalo National Park are exempt from mandatory registration of fisher, lynx, otter and wolverine and from the provincial export permit for those species.
license_summary.report_violation: Report A Poacher: 1-800-642-3800 (24 hours a day, 7 days a week), or online at alberta.ca/report-poacher. Report violations on public land or in provincial parks to 310-LAND; emergencies 9-1-1.
license_summary.resident_licence: An Alberta resident aged 14 or older may obtain a Resident Fur Management Licence ($20) to hunt or trap furbearing animals on land they own, lease (other than a lease within an RFMA) or occupy, or on other private land with the owner/occupant's written permission on Form WA 19A, which must be carried with the licence. Resident FML holders may NOT take fisher, otter, lynx or wolverine anywhere in Alberta, and may not take marten in Fur Management Zone 3.
license_summary.rfma_system: Alberta has approximately 1,630 Registered Fur Management Areas (the Guide's licensing page says approximately 1,632; its 2025/26 statistics say 1,628) — parcels of public (Crown) land whose boundaries are described on the Registered Fur Management Licence. The senior holder is authorized for a five-year term and must renew the licence each year on or before September 30, submitting the Registered Fur Harvest Report (Form WA12); failure to renew may result in revocation of RFML privileges. The senior holder may add partners under a Fur Management Area Partnership Agreement approved in writing by a wildlife biologist; partnership agreements are confirmed annually, and partners are issued a licence and a wallet-size WA188 card valid July 1 to June 30. The senior holder's spouse, or a resident child under 18 of the senior holder, may hunt or trap on the RFMA without a licence, with the harvest included in the senior holder's WA12. A senior holder may transfer an RFMA by conditional relinquishment, in person at a government office. An RFML authorizes hunting and trapping only on the holder's RFMA(s) or on lands the holder owns, leases or occupies; a Resident Fur Management Licence is required for other private lands.
license_summary.trap_check: Every non-killing trap must be examined at least once every 24 hours when set under a Resident Fur Management Licence, and at least once every 48 hours in any other case (i.e. under a Registered Fur Management Licence) (Wildlife Regulation, s. 110).
license_summary.trapping_licence: A fur management licence is required to hunt or trap furbearing animals in Alberta under the Wildlife Act and the Wildlife Regulation (Alberta Regulation 143/1997), except under the no-licence problem-wildlife authorities and for non-licence animals (raccoon and skunk). A fur management licence or trapper's identification card must be carried at all times while trapping.
license_summary.youth: A resident under 18 whose parent holds a Registered Fur Management Licence (senior holder or partner) may hunt or trap in that RFMA subject to seasons, quotas and restrictions; residents aged 12 to 17 may trap under the senior holder's direct supervision with the senior holder's permission and written parent/guardian authorization. A resident under 16 whose parent holds a Resident Fur Management Licence may hunt or trap on the parent's lands (the WA 19A lands); residents aged 12 to 13 may hunt or trap under the licence holder's direct supervision with the holder's permission and written parent/guardian authorization.

verification.confirmation_notes: All 120 cells of the fur season table (15 Table 5 species x 8 Fur Management Zones) were verified twice: in the Alberta Guide to Trapping Regulations 2026-2027 (p. 15; online edition at albertaregulations.ca/trappingregs/quotas-seasons.html) and in the law itself, Wildlife Regulation (Alberta Regulation 143/1997), Schedule 15, Table 5, King's Printer consolidation current as of September 17, 2026 (amendments to AR 234/2026). The two sources agree on every date and every CLOSED cell. Licence fees were cross-checked between the Guide's Licence Fees table and Schedule 8, Part 3 of the Regulation and agree exactly. Trap rules were cross-checked between the Guide's General Regulations and Regulation ss. 107, 107.1, 108, 109, 109.1, 110 and 115; problem-wildlife authorities between the Guide's Control of Problem Wildlife page and Schedule 1, s. 7 of the Regulation; registration and reporting rules against the Guide's licensing, quotas/seasons and furbearer-management pages. Relative dates were computed for 2026-27 and verified by calendar check: February 15, 2027 is a Monday, and February 2027 has 28 days (2027 is not a leap year), so 'the last day of February' in the resident bobcat hunting season (Schedule 15, s. 8(6)) is February 28, 2027. Three Guide-vs-Regulation detail differences were found — the Guide merges the Regulation's Table 5 footnotes 4 and 5, compresses the otter WMU list, and misstates the laminated-jaw thickness as 8 mm where the Regulation says 9 mm — and are recorded in known_gaps; in each case the dataset follows the Regulation.
known_gaps: Current RFMA open-season quota values for otter, wolverine, lynx and fisher (Wildlife Regulation, Schedule 15, s. 8.7) were not located. A quota set by the Minister must be made publicly available on a department website, but no quota figures appear in the 2026-27 Guide — which no longer prints the RFMA limits table (a basic limit per RFMA plus per-township increments) that appeared in guides up to at least 2018-19 and was still listed in the 2020-21 Guide's table of contents — and no quota page was found in this pass. Resolution: Alberta Forestry and Parks department website or a Fish and Wildlife District Office. Until resolved, the dataset records the quota mechanism, not numbers.

Fur Management Zone composition: the Guide's p. 17 map shows which WMUs make up each FMZ only as a graphic; no official text list of FMZ-to-WMU membership was transcribed in this pass. WMUs are legally described in Schedule 9 of the Wildlife Regulation (hundreds of boundary descriptions). Resolution: transcribe from the Guide map or obtain a department FMZ boundary dataset before building any zone picker.

Laminated-jaw thickness discrepancy: the 2026-27 Guide's summary of the leg-hold trap rules describes laminated jaws as two steel parallel jaws 'at least 8 mm' thick; Wildlife Regulation s. 107(3) says 9 mm. The Regulation governs and the dataset follows it (9 mm); the Guide figure appears to be a summary error.

The 2026-27 Guide's season-table footnote 4 merges two distinct legal footnotes. In Wildlife Regulation Schedule 15, Table 5, footnote 4 (red/Arctic fox: October 1 to February 15 in WMUs 524, 532, 534, 536 and 539) and footnote 5 (marten, mink, fisher and wolverine: November 1 to February 15 in the same WMUs) are separate. The dataset follows the Regulation, so the fox extension row opens October 1 while the marten/mink/fisher/wolverine extension rows open November 1.

The Guide's otter footnote 6 compresses the FMZ 4 application area to 'WMUs 330, 336 to 360'; Wildlife Regulation Schedule 15, Table 5, footnote 7 enumerates the specific units (330, 336, 337, 338, 339, 340, 342, 344, 346, 347, 348, 349, 350, 351, 352, 353, 354, 355, 356, 360, 507, 508, 521). The dataset follows the Regulation's enumerated list.

Recreational (non-trapper) hunting seasons under the Alberta Guide to Hunting Regulations 2026 — including general wolf and coyote hunting seasons and black bear season dates — were not scoped in this pass. This dataset covers the trapping guide plus the problem-wildlife (no-licence) hunting authorities in Wildlife Regulation Schedule 1, s. 7 and the resident bobcat hunting season in Schedule 15, s. 8(6).

It is not listed in Schedule 6 of the Wildlife Regulation (endangered and threatened animals). The dataset models the season exactly as written in Table 5.

aihts.note: Alberta implements the AIHTS in law: Wildlife Regulation (AR 143/1997) s. 107.1 incorporates Phase 1 of the competent authority's 'Certified Traps – AIHTS Implementation' document — the Fur Institute of Canada certified-trap list — by reference into the Regulation, and provides that a person shall not use any trap for a certified species unless the trap is currently listed by name and certified for that species. The Minister delegates amendment of the list to the competent authority and must publish the implementation list annually in the Alberta Guide to Trapping Regulations. 'Alberta has agreed to implement the AIHTS standards' (Guide, General Regulations).

phase_2_certified_not_yet_mandatory.note: Phase 2 certified foothold restraining traps for coyote; they become mandatory beginning with the 2028/29 trapping season (Guide, Important Changes).

Phase 2 certified cage and box traps for raccoon (Havahart, Ramconct, Tomahawk models). Although listed as Phase 2 in the Guide's trap lists, the Guide's Important Changes state they are mandatory beginning with the 2026/27 season — treat as mandatory for 2026-27.

trap_rules: Only traps currently listed by name as certified for a species may be used for that species (Wildlife Regulation, s. 107.1(2)); it is unlawful to use traps that do not meet the AIHTS standards for a certified species (Guide, General Regulations).
Traps set for fur-bearing animals must be killing devices, leg snares, or live-container (cage/box) traps (Wildlife Regulation, s. 107(1)).

Leg-hold traps may be used only as killing devices, except for wolf, coyote, lynx, bobcat and raccoon, where they may also be used as restraining devices if the jaws are laminated (two steel parallel jaws, each at least 9 mm thick), offset, or padded (Wildlife Regulation, s. 107(3)). The 2026-27 Guide's summary of this rule says 8 mm; the Regulation says 9 mm and governs (see verification.known_gaps). Section 107 does not apply to fox (s. 107(4)).
Foothold traps with toothed jaws, or with an inside jaw spread of 23 cm (9 in.) or more, may not be used to trap furbearing animals (Guide, General Regulations).

A foothold trap that is not set as a killing device may not be set in a tree or on a pole (Wildlife Regulation, s. 108), and foothold traps not set as killing devices may be used only for bobcat, coyote, fox, lynx or wolf; every other furbearer must be taken in a killing device or a live-container trap (Guide, General Regulations).

Neck snares must have a locking device that prevents the snare from loosening once an animal is caught, except snares set underwater and single-strand wire snares for squirrel, rabbit or hare (Wildlife Regulation, s. 109).

New for 2026-27: a trapper who sets a baited killing neck snare within 200 m of the boundary of land occupied as a dwelling must notify the occupant (Wildlife Regulation, s. 109.1, added by AR 187/2026); the requirement does not apply where the adjacent land is larger than a quarter section.

Trap check: every non-killing trap must be examined at least once every 24 hours when set under a Resident Fur Management Licence, and at least once every 48 hours in any other case (i.e. under a Registered Fur Management Licence) (Wildlife Regulation, s. 110).

Snares may be used only under a Registered Fur Management Licence, or under a Resident Fur Management Licence for bobcat, coyote, fox, squirrel and wolf, and for beaver where the snare loop is completely underwater; a resident may also snare rabbit and hare with single-strand wire of 20 gauge or heavier and a loop diameter of 13 cm (5 in.) or less (Guide, General Regulations).

Seasonal snaring restriction: from October 1 to November 30, snaring of coyote, fox and wolf is prohibited in Fur Management Zones 4, 5 and 6 except in WMUs 314, 316, 318, 320, 322, 324, 330, 332, 334, 336, 337, 338, 348, 360, 410, 412, 414, 416, 417, 418, 507, 508 and 521 (Wildlife Regulation, Schedule 15, s. 9(1)(f)).

Slide-wire (drowning) sets must have a lock, must be anchored securely, and must be set in water deep enough to completely submerge the largest animal that may enter the trap (Guide, General Regulations).

Certified cage and box traps are mandatory for raccoon beginning with the 2026/27 season; certified foothold restraining traps for coyote become mandatory beginning with the 2028/29 season (Guide, Important Changes for 2026-27).

Trapping is prohibited in ecological reserves and, with limited RFMA exceptions, in wildlife sanctuaries; no furbearer may be harvested within 100 m of Highway 1A in WMU 410 except with traps. No person may remove, spring or otherwise interfere with another person's traps, except that a Registered FML holder may remove unlawful traps within their own RFMA and must report it immediately. Poison (except as authorized under the Agricultural Pests Act) and sharp hooks may not be used (Guide, General Regulations; Wildlife Regulation).

aihts.canada_wide: AIHTS in force in Canada since 1 June 1999 (Canada, the EU and Russia are parties; the US is not a party). FIC-certified traps mandatory per Phase 1 lists - killing traps: beaver, Canada lynx & bobcat, fisher, marten, muskrat (on land and underwater), otter, raccoon, weasels/ermine; restraining traps: beaver (cage), bobcat, Canada lynx, raccoon, wolf. Conventional steel-jawed leghold restraining traps on land are effectively banned for AIHTS species. Killing neck snares are NOT AIHTS traps and are not FIC-certified; provinces regulate snares separately. [R1 s.2a]
aihts.jurisdiction_specific: Certified cage/box traps for raccoon mandatory from 2026-27; certified coyote restraining traps mandatory from 2028-29. Alberta guide: jaw-type leg/foothold restraining traps on land prohibited for badger, beaver, ermine, fisher, marten, muskrat and otter; conventional steel-jawed legholds on land prohibited for bobcat, coyote, lynx, raccoon and wolf - only certified/modified restraining traps for that group. [R1 s.2a]

check_interval.live_holding: Non-killing devices: 48 hours under a Registered Fur Management Licence; 24 hours under a Resident Fur Management Licence.
check_interval.killing: No legal check requirement for killing devices.

canada_only.tenure: Registered Fur Management Areas (~1,632 RFMAs; Senior Holder on a 5-year term, licence renewed annually by Sept 30) plus a separate Resident Fur Management Licence for private land and some non-RFMA public land.
canada_only.trap_id_requirement: None found - no trap owner-ID marking requirement in the sources searched (follow-up pass, Nov 17); identification runs through licence/tenure and pelt seals instead. Near-miss: black bear bait stations need a sign showing the owner's name or RFMA number - a bait-site sign, not a trap mark.
canada_only.royalty: None found in the current Wildlife Act, Wildlife Regulation AR 143/97, or the 2025-26 Guide to Trapping Regulations. [R2 Item 5]
canada_only.nuisance_route: Paid route exists - Damage Control Licence (Fish and Wildlife Stewardship): lethal control of specified wildlife causing/likely to cause damage or safety threats, typically valid ~1 month; never issued for capture/relocation, general nuisance, or population control. Counties hold DCLs and appoint contract trappers as external designates for problem beaver; some counties employ Problem Wildlife Specialists. [R1 s.4]
canada_only.harvest_reporting_and_sealing: Mandatory registration at a Fish & Wildlife office for fisher, lynx, otter, wolverine and all bobcat (wolverine skull must be delivered with the pelt). Fur Harvest Reports are required for annual licence renewal; Senior RFMA holders are additionally requested (voluntary) to submit logbooks to the Alberta Furbearer Harvest Program. [R1 s.5]
